items.title: A Lapel Pin Fuels Chinese Talk of a China-Russia-Iran Triangle
items.author: Rudy Lu
items.creator: Rudy Lu
items.summary: In China’s tightly managed political information environment, seemingly trivial interactions between senior officials can become material for close reading. Netizens and commentators scrutinize seconds-long clips — who smiles, who initiates a handshake, how firmly leaders grip hands or whether they appear unusually relaxed around one …
items.summary_source: The China-Global South Project source metadata
items.body:
In China’s tightly managed political information environment, seemingly trivial interactions between senior officials can become material for close reading. Netizens and commentators scrutinize seconds-long clips — who smiles, who initiates a handshake, how firmly leaders grip hands or whether they appear unusually relaxed around one another — for clues about relationships that official readouts rarely reveal.

A brief encounter between the foreign ministers of China, Russia and Iran at the BRICS summit has become the latest example.

Video from the sidelines of the summit in New Delhi showed Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi chatting and laughing with his Russian and Iranian counterparts Sergei Lavrov and Abbas Araghchi. At one point, Wang reached toward a pin on Araghchi’s jacket, prompting the Iranian foreign minister to laugh. 

Araghchi’s official Telegram channel later posted a close-up of the exchange , identifying the pin as an emblem depicting the map of Iran.

The moment quickly spread across Chinese social media, landing on the trending search list of Weibo, a Chinese social media platform often compared to X, under “Wang Yi helps the Iranian foreign minister straighten his pin” (#王毅帮伊朗外长整理胸针).

A wave of Chinese-language amplification followed.

Nationalist commentary account Rongping (戎评) described Iran as “holding the advantage” and in high spirits, with China and Russia sharing the mood. 

“Such a personal and warm interaction between the Chinese and Iranian foreign ministers sends a strong signal to the outside world: China-Iran relations have long gone beyond a simple exchange of interests, and the two sides share a high degree of familiarity and trust,” it wrote.

Another online commentary said the seemingly insignificant gesture reflected a shift in the international balance of power that would make the White House “deeply uncomfortable.”

“U.S. pressure is pushing the three sides closer together,” it said. “Washington can continue to pressure the three countries separately, but it will find it increasingly difficult to stop them from exchanging resources, coordinating positions and jointly seeking alternatives.”

It said Beijing could keep channels open to Gulf Arab countries, and Moscow could draw on its close strategic ties with Tehran. Working through BRICS, the three could help Iran break its diplomatic isolation and avert a complete rupture with the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states.

Those interpretations, however, largely reflect one strand of domestic online opinion that is sympathetic to Iran and distrustful of the United States. Beijing’s official posture has been more carefully calibrated, especially ahead of Xi Jinping’s scheduled Sept. 24 meeting with Trump in Washington.

Araghchi traveled to Beijing on Sep. 16 for talks with Wang Yi. The Chinese Foreign Ministry described Iran as a “comprehensive strategic partner” and said Beijing was prepared to help safeguard Tehran’s “legitimate rights and interests.” 

But much of Wang’s message focused on containing the conflict. He urged Iran and the United States to exercise restraint and return to negotiations, backed dialogue between Tehran and Gulf Arab governments, called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and warned against the fighting spreading toward Yemen and the Red Sea.

China’s balancing role was also evident when Saudi Arabia asked Beijing to press Iran to rein in the Houthis, Reuters reported, citing three Iranian sources . China then privately urged Tehran to use its influence over the Yemeni group, whose advances threatened Saudi oil exports and shipping through the Red Sea — a vital route for Chinese trade.

items.body:
SK Hynix Is Eyeing Intel’s (INTC) Ohio Site. Why Micron (MU) Should Pay Attention

Habib Ur Rehman
September 22, 2026 3 min read

INTC
-0.56%

SKHY
+0.84%

MU
-2.05%

Explore stocks on Coinbase Trading disclosure

Trading disclosure The above button links to Coinbase. Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational.
Learn more

SK Hynix is exploring something it has never done before: manufacturing memory chips in the United States.
Reuters reported on September 16 that the Korean memory giant is discussing several possibilities with Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC ), including leasing part of Intel's long-delayed Ohio complex or forming a venture involving Intel and large cloud customers. SK Hynix said no specific plan has been finalized.
For Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU ), the talks matter because one of its strongest strategic advantages is being the major U.S.-based memory producer while AI has made DRAM and HBM increasingly scarce.

SK Hynix May Move Into Intel’s $100 Billion Ohio Fab. Micron Has a Reason to Watch SK Hynix Could Give Intel Another Path for Its Delayed Ohio Site Intel has committed enormous capital to Ohio, with the broader project potentially reaching around $100 billion over time. Delays have pushed planned production into the next decade. A tenant or joint-venture partner could therefore help Intel share the financial burden of developing the Ohio site rather than relying entirely on its own foundry demand to justify the buildout.

That is the bull case. The bear case is that exploratory talks are a long way from revenue. Bringing advanced Korean memory production to the U.S. could face cost problems, technology-transfer restrictions and objections from Seoul. Intel still needs its core manufacturing roadmap to work.
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) sits on the other side of the equation. AI demand has pushed memory pricing and availability into a strong cycle, and Micron is already pursuing a large U.S. manufacturing expansion. More domestic manufacturing incentives and customer interest in secure supply support that plan.
A successful SK Hynix move could eventually erode part of Micron's U.S.-supply differentiation. U.S. cloud companies would gain another potential domestic supplier, while additional long-term memory capacity could eventually loosen the market that currently supports exceptional pricing.
Hedge funds loaded up on both chipmakers Insider Monkey tracked 138 hedge funds holding Intel in Q2, up sharply from 112 in Q1. AQR Capital Management held roughly 10.7 million shares after trimming its stake about 7%. Micron's count rose to 184 funds from 154, one of the stronger quarter-over-quarter increases among large semiconductor names. Coatue Management expanded its MU stake dramatically during the quarter.

Intel had about 152.2 million shares sold short as of August 31, roughly 3% of public float and 1.7 days to cover.
The talks do not rescue Intel's foundry strategy or weaken Micron overnight. They do show what AI scarcity is doing to the supply chain. Memory manufacturing is becoming strategic enough that SK Hynix is considering putting advanced capacity on American soil, and Intel's delayed Ohio project suddenly gives it a potentially valuable asset to negotiate with.

Story Continues
While we acknowledge the potential of INTC and MU as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. items.title: How one millennial is building wealth by buying assets, not stuff
items.author: Hani Richter
items.creator: Hani Richter
items.summary: Some are figuring out how to turn reselling into a source of income.
items.body:
Dandan Zhu. Courtesy Dandan Zhu/Handout via REUTERS When Dandan Zhu purchased a Rolex in 2012 for $2,400, she didn’t just treat it like a luxury watch —she saw it as an asset.
Years later, that investment paid off. When her tenants failed to pay rent on time, Zhu sold the Rolex and broke even, giving her a quick influx of cash to cover her mortgage.
“I deeply understand retail arbitrage,” the New York-based 38-year-old says, referring to the practice of reselling goods for a profit. As a university student, she sold gaming consoles on eBay to help pay off her tuition. Even after graduating in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and landing her first job in recruitment, she continued buying and reselling goods to supplement her income, eventually climbing the career ladder and purchasing her first home in 2014.
Nowadays, the former headhunter-turned-content creator trades primarily in limited-edition luxury bags that she knows will retain value and, if needed, generate income. “I specifically know specific products I can guarantee a $2,000 profit,” she says, noting that while basic bags will depreciate in value, "the ones that will appreciate are those (that are) very special.”
Dandan Zhu. Courtesy Dandan Zhu/Handout via REUTERS While she researches products online and in-store, Zhu says she also relies on AI to help her identify which items are likely to appreciate in value in the longterm.
THE WIDER TREND
A 2026 ThredUp and GlobalData Resale Report found that more than half of Gen Z and millennial consumers browse or prioritize second-hand purchases before buying new.
Cory Christiana, a Boston-based certified financial planner and investment adviser at NEXTEN FP, sees this trend as generational. “Each generation sees what the generation did before and tends to set their own path,” he says, noting that while boomers accumulated homes and financial assets, younger generations, facing affordability challenges and lives increasingly lived online, may be drawn towards more physical assets.
“It’s important to slow down and ask yourself if there is real value in a purchase or if it's something you want,” he says. “The distinction is an important one.”
Historically, certain jewelry, collectible cars, and artwork have retained and grown in value over time. But Christiana emphasizes that these kinds of assets work best as additions to a diversified portfolio — including stocks, bonds, real estate and cash — rather than as a replacement for them.
KEY TAKEAWAYS
A luxury item can function as emergency liquidity. When Zhu's tenants stopped paying rent and she had little working capital, the Rolex she sold gave her something she could convert into cash when she needed it.
Research before buying. Check realistic resale prices and total transaction costs before treating a purchase as an asset. It’s important to note that an item only qualifies as an asset if it is rare and other people are willing to pay for it. A limited-edition watch or handbag fits this criterion; mass-produced goods for fast fashion, however, typically do not.
Investing in assets works well within a diverse financial plan. Treat resalable assets as an addition to a wider portfolio of investments, not a replacement.
Have a money lesson or story to share? Tell us what worked for you — or what didn’t — by emailing hani.richter@tr.com .

items.title: Who are the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen?
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the start of a military counteroffensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
items.body:
Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the start of a [USN:L1N45Q02D TEXT:"military counteroffensive"] against the Iran-backed Houthis, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
Renewed warfare between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has reignited Yemen's frozen civil war and heightened risks to Red Sea shipping, further disrupting Middle Eastern energy exports already choked by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz.
WHO ARE THE HOUTHIS? The Houthis are a military, political and religious movement that rules over most of northwest Yemen and has [USN:L6N43M0M9 TEXT:"disrupted global trade and energy"] markets with attacks on cargo ships and tankers in the Red Sea.
It began firing on ships in the Red Sea and launching drones and missiles at Israel in November 2023, saying it was doing so in support of Palestinians during Israel's war in Gaza that began the previous month.
Those attacks on Red Sea shipping, as well as on Saudi Arabia, resumed this year in response to the United States' war on the Houthis' close ally Iran.
WHAT DO THE HOUTHIS WANT? The group emerged in far north Yemen in the 1990s as a revival movement for the Zaydi sect of Shi'ite Islam, which had once ruled Yemen but whose northern heartland had become impoverished and marginalised.
It fought a series of guerrilla wars against Yemen's national army and a brief border conflict with Sunni Saudi Arabia.
When Yemen's longtime president Ali Abdullah Saleh was brought down in the 2011 "Arab spring" protests, the group consolidated its control over northern Yemen, rejecting a Gulf-backed political transition.
With Iranian support, the group's secretive leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, was meanwhile turning his faction of mountain fighters into a force of tens of thousands.
In 2014 they seized the capital Sanaa, driving the internationally recognised government south towards Aden.
WHAT'S BEHIND THE HOUTHI CONFLICT WITH SAUDI ARABIA? Fearful of growing Iranian influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in early 2015 to dislodge the group, restore the government and revive the transition plan.
The resulting [USN:L6N3Y307N TEXT:"civil war"] triggered one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of bitter fighting and devastating airstrikes by Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners, including the United Arab Emirates.
However, neither side was able to gain much ground in Yemen's mountainous terrain, and the Houthis remained in control over the northwest, where most of the population lives.
They demonstrated significant missile and drone capabilities, attacking oil installations and vital infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
After years of fighting, the UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that maintained peace until this year.
HOW MUCH DAMAGE CAN THE HOUTHIS DO WITH ATTACKS IN THE RED SEA AND SAUDI ARABIA? The group's attacks on Red Sea shipping between 2023 and 2025 significantly disrupted global trade, forcing cargo ships travelling between Europe and Asia to take a long, expensive route around Africa.
Their threats to oil tankers during the Iran war have added to the squeeze on energy out of the Gulf after Tehran mostly choked off the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a global oil crisis.
Some Houthi missile and drone attacks have caused significant damage in Saudi Arabia and the UAE over the years, but have proven less effective against targets further north, such as Israel.
LINKS WITH IRAN Iran champions the Houthis as part of its regional "Axis of Resistance", which also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iraqi Shi'ite militias, though its ties with the Yemeni movement are less clear than with those other groups.
The Houthis do not recognise Iran's supreme leader as their ultimate religious authority in the same way Hezbollah and the Iraqi groups do. Their motivations are also mainly domestic, though they are ideologically aligned with Iran.
The US says Iran has armed, funded and trained the Houthis with help from Hezbollah. The Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy and say they develop their own weapons.

4 octobre (Reuters) - Le président yéménite, dont le gouvernement est soutenu par l'Arabie saoudite, a annoncé dimanche le lancement d'une vaste opération militaire contre les rebelles houthis pro-iraniens, visant à reprendre le contrôle des territoires qu'ils occupent.
Des explosions entendues pendant la visite du chancelier allemand à Kyiv
KYIV, 4 octobre (Reuters) - Des sirènes d'alerte aérienne et des explosions ont retenti dimanche dans la capitale ukrainienne, Kyiv, alors que le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz rendait visite au président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky dans le cadre du renouvellement du soutien de l'Allemagne à l'Ukraine.
Éthiopie-La capitale du Tigré sous contrôle des forces gouvernementales-sources
4 octobre (Reuters) - Les forces gouvernementales éthiopiennes et les milices alliées ont repris le contrôle de la capitale du Tigré, ont rapporté à Reuters trois sources dimanche, infligeant ainsi un revers majeur à l'alliance d'opposition qui gouverne cette région du nord.
Les Brésiliens se rendent aux urnes dans un contexte de forte polarisation
BRASILIA/SÃO PAULO, 4 octobre (Reuters) - Les Brésiliens se rendront aux urnes dimanche pour le premier tour d'une élection annoncée très serrée, après une campagne marquée par des scandales de corruption, des inquiétudes économiques et des accusations d'ingérence américaine.
Espagne-Deux morts dans des inondations en Catalogne
4 octobre (Reuters) - Deux personnes ont péri et une autre est portée disparue à la suite de fortes pluies et d'inondations dans la région de Catalogne, en Espagne, ont rapporté dimanche les autorités.
Le Premier ministre letton en passe de diriger une coalition pro-ukrainienne
RIGA, 4 octobre (Reuters) - Le Premier ministre letton, Andris Kulbergs, devrait conserver le pouvoir, sa "Liste unie", formation centriste et pro-ukrainienne, étant en passe de signer une large victoire, la plus importante aux élections législatives depuis que la Lettonie a retrouvé son indépendance en 1991.
L'Ukraine va intensifier ses frappes sur les raffineries russes
KYIV, 3 octobre (Reuters) - L'Ukraine va intensifier ses attaques contre les raffineries russes en réponse à la nouvelle stratégie de frappes aériennes menée par Moscou visant à forcer la population à quitter Kyiv et d'autres villes, sans pour autant prendre pour cible les civils, a déclaré le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky.
La Russie continuera à pilonner Kyiv, invite les diplomates à quitter la capitale ukrainienne
3 octobre (Reuters) - La Russie a déclaré samedi qu'elle continuerait à mener des frappes sur Kyiv et d'autres villes ukrainiennes, exhortant les ressortissants étrangers et les diplomates à quitter la capitale ukrainienne.
USA/MIDTERMS-Trump tente de mobiliser les électeurs dans l'Ohio
VANDALIA, Ohio, 3 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a adopté un ton combatif lors d'un rassemblement organisé samedi dans l'Ohio, l'un des Etats où le scrutin pour remporter un siège au Sénat lors des élections de mi-mandat pourrait être décisif.
Le copilote de Flydubai a tenté de commettre un "attentat" avec une hache - procureur
Le copilote du vol FZ1073 de Flydubai, à destination d'Israël, a tenté de commettre un "attentat terroriste" pendant le vol avec une hache se trouvant dans le cockpit, a déclaré samedi le procureur général des Emirats arabes unis.
